title: CyberAv3ngers
summary: CyberAv3ngers is a label used by public authorities and vendors for an Iran-nexus cluster that became known for intrusions into internet-exposed operational technology, particularly programmable logic controllers and the operator display panels attached to them in water and wastewater systems. The reported approach is not deep exploitation of industrial control networks; the group targets devices reachable directly from the internet that still use default or weak credentials and were never designed to be exposed. Once connected, operators have been reported to change device configuration, alter the text shown on displays, and disrupt monitoring, which produces visible effects without any destructive capability. Government advisories state their own attribution and confidence levels, and analysts outside government describe the cluster more cautiously. Evidence is strongest at the network edge: connection records for internet-facing controllers, successful authentication from unexpected addresses, configuration changes on the device, and unusual project file downloads.

beginner.definition: CyberAv3ngers is a name for a group of attackers that public reports link to Iran. The group attacks small industrial computers that control things like water pumps and valves. These computers are called programmable logic controllers, or PLCs for short. The attackers often get in because the device still uses its factory password.
beginner.whyItMatters: Water and power systems keep daily life running. When an attacker changes what a controller displays or does, real people can lose service. Many of these devices were built to be simple, not secure. If they are connected to the internet, anyone can try the factory password. This group shows that a small mistake in a control room can have a large effect.
howItWorks: The attackers search the internet for industrial devices that anyone outside can reach.
They try the factory password, which many owners never change after the first setup.
If it works, they can see the same screens that operators use every day.
They may change the words on those screens or stop the equipment from working.
They also look for other devices on the same network to reach more sites.
Because the devices are simple, they often keep no useful record of the visit.
beginner.example: Imagine a small village water tower with a control box on the outside wall. The box has a keypad, and a sticker with the factory code is still attached. The engineers trust the box because it is old and simple. One morning the display shows a rude message instead of water levels. The pumps still work, but nobody can read the system. The lesson is plain: a door that opens onto the street needs a new lock and a fence.
takeaways: Change factory passwords on every device, especially control equipment.
Keep industrial devices off the public internet, behind a protected connection.
Write down what each device should display, so changes are easy to spot.

objectives: Explain what CyberAv3ngers is and why internet-exposed controllers are its main target.
Describe how default credentials create risk in operational technology environments.
Identify the log sources that record access to an industrial controller.
Explain the difference between an intrusion that disrupts displays and one that damages equipment.
Summarise network design choices that remove control devices from the public internet.
Describe how public advisories state attribution and how to report that confidence accurately.
